title: Berkeley
orientation: Russell examines George Berkeley (1685-1753), famous for denying the existence of matter while insisting that sensible things remain real because God perpetually perceives them. Focusing on the Dialogues of Hylas and Philonous, Russell reconstructs Berkeley's arguments that we perceive only sensible qualities, not 'things,' and that these qualities are mind-dependent -- then subjects Berkeley's reasoning to detailed logical and empirical criticism, distinguishing what Russell thinks Berkeley actually proved (that we perceive qualities, relative to the percipient) from what Berkeley thought he had proved (that all reality is mental).
historical_background: Berkeley, an Irishman, became a Fellow of Trinity College, Dublin, at twenty-two; all his philosophically important works -- A New Theory of Vision (1709), The Principles of Human Knowledge (1710), and the Dialogues of Hylas and Philonous (1713) -- were written before he was thirty. He later travelled to Rhode Island (1728-31) pursuing an unrealized scheme for a college in Bermuda (the town of Berkeley, California, is named after him, from his line 'Westward the course of empire takes its way'), became Bishop of Cloyne in 1734, and in later life turned from philosophy to promoting tar-water as a medicinal cure-all.
philosophical_problems: Do we ever perceive 'material things' as such, or only sensible qualities (colours, sounds, tastes) associated with them?
Are sensible qualities -- and, more controversially, 'primary' qualities like extension and motion -- inherently mental, or could they exist independently of any perceiving mind?
If material objects exist only through being perceived, what accounts for their continuous existence when no finite mind is observing them?
What, precisely, does it mean to say that something is 'perceived,' and can meaningful sense be given to the idea of an unperceived event?
Can any coherent meaning be given to the terms 'mind' and 'matter' once the traditional notion of substance is rejected?

philosophers_discussed.name: George Berkeley
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's sole primary subject, referred to in his own Dialogues under the character 'Philonous': Russell reconstructs his arguments against the existence of matter, his use of God to secure the continuity of unperceived objects, and subjects both his logical and empirical arguments to sustained critical analysis.

philosophers_discussed.name: John Locke
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Referenced throughout as the target whose primary/secondary quality distinction Berkeley's arguments extend and radicalize -- Berkeley (via the character Hylas) begins by defending Locke's distinction before being argued out of it entirely by Philonous.

philosophers_discussed.name: G. E. Moore
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited for his criticism of idealists as effectively holding that 'trains only have wheels while they are in stations,' used by Russell to illustrate common sense's resistance to idealism about unperceived objects.

philosophers_discussed.name: Arthur Eddington
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as a modern representative of the view that we may reasonably infer events analogous to our own experience (e.g., other people's sensations) without extending this to wholly unperceived, mind-independent events.

philosophers_discussed.name: G. W. F. Hegel
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named, alongside Berkeley, as holding (on different grounds) that there are logical reasons proving only minds and mental events can exist -- a view Russell calls 'a complete mistake.'

core_concepts.name: The denial of the existence of matter
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Berkeley argued there is no such thing as 'matter' existing independently of minds. What we call material objects -- trees, rocks, tables -- are really just collections ('bundles') of sensible qualities (colours, sounds, textures) that exist only insofar as they are perceived by some mind.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Berkeley 'maintained that material objects only exist through being perceived' (esse est percipi); the reality of sensible things 'consists in being perceived,' against the common-sense view (voiced by the character Hylas) that 'to exist is one thing, and to be perceived is another.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is Berkeley's most famous and radical doctrine, supported, Russell argues, by 'a number of ingenious arguments' -- though Russell contends the arguments actually establish a more modest conclusion (that we perceive only relative, mind-dependent qualities, not that all reality is mental).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed principally in The Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) and dramatized in the Dialogues of Hylas and Philonous (1713).
examples: Ronald Knox's limerick about the tree in the quad and its reply ('I am always about in the Quad... GOD')
The claim that a table is nothing but its visual shape, hardness, sound when rapped, and smell -- with no additional 'substance' behind these qualities
objections: Russell's central objection: Berkeley's arguments prove qualities are perceiver-relative, not that they are 'mental' in any well-defined sense, since Berkeley never adequately defines 'mental'
competing_positions: Common-sense/scientific realism (voiced by Hylas), which holds material substance exists independently of perception
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Provoked a long line of philosophical responses and refutations; Russell notes 'to refute him has been ... a favourite pastime among metaphysicians,' foreshadowing his own treatment of Hume in the next chapter.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: God's constant perception of all things is what, for Berkeley, secures the continuous existence of the physical world -- making this a 'weighty argument,' in Berkeley's own view, for God's existence.

core_concepts.name: God as guarantor of the continuity of unperceived objects
core_concepts.plain_explanation: If things only exist while being perceived, a tree would seem to blink in and out of existence depending on whether anyone is looking at it. Berkeley's solution: God is always perceiving everything, everywhere, so objects have a continuous existence even when no human is looking.
core_concepts.precise_definition: To the objection that unobserved objects (e.g., a tree with no one in the quad) would cease to exist, Berkeley replies that 'God always perceives everything'; without God, physical objects 'would have a jerky life, suddenly leaping into being when we look at them,' but God's constant perception secures their continuity as ordinary common sense supposes.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Berkeley treats this need for a perpetual perceiver as itself a proof of God's existence, tightly binding his metaphysics of perception to natural theology.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out across the Principles and Dialogues; popularly immortalized in Ronald Knox's limerick and its reply, which Russell quotes in full.
examples: The Knox limerick: 'There was a young man who said, \"God / Must think it exceedingly odd ...\"' and its reply, 'I am always about in the Quad ... GOD.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological: continuity of the physical world becomes evidence for God's constant, universal perception.

core_concepts.name: The Dialogues' method: Hylas and Philonous
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Berkeley presents his argument as a conversation between two characters: Hylas, who represents ordinary scientific common sense (belief in material substance), and Philonous, who is Berkeley's own mouthpiece, gradually arguing Hylas out of his belief in matter step by step, quality by quality.
core_concepts.precise_definition: In the Dialogues of Hylas and Philonous, Philonous leads Hylas through a sequence of arguments -- first about secondary qualities (heat/cold, taste, smell, sound, colour), then about primary qualities (extension, figure, motion) -- each time showing that what Hylas thought was an objective property of matter is in fact relative to, and dependent on, the perceiver.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this dialectical structure as pedagogically powerful and 'most persuasively set forth,' but focuses his analysis specifically on 'the first [dialogue] and the very beginning of the second,' judging the remainder 'of minor importance.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: The Dialogues of Hylas and Philonous, 1713.
examples: The lukewarm water argument: one hand hot, one cold, both placed in the same lukewarm water, which feels hot to one hand and cold to the other -- proving, Berkeley argues, that heat/cold cannot be objectively 'in' the water
The sunset-clouds argument: clouds are red and gold from a distance but colourless up close, showing colour is not simply 'in' the object
The near/far argument: things look larger when close and smaller when far, showing size (a primary quality) is also perceiver-relative

core_concepts.name: Russell's critique: qualities are relative, not necessarily 'mental'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell agrees with Berkeley that we perceive only qualities (not some extra hidden 'thing' behind them), and that these qualities depend on the perceiver's situation. But he disputes Berkeley's further claim that this makes the qualities 'mental,' arguing Berkeley never properly defines what 'mental' means and simply assumes everything must be either wholly material or wholly mental.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's assessment: 'His reasoning is completely cogent as to the first point [we perceive qualities, not things], but as to the second [that these qualities are mental] it suffers from the absence of any definition of the word \"mental.\"' Berkeley 'relies, in fact, upon the received view that everything must be either material or mental, and that nothing is both.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This distinction lets Russell salvage what he regards as Berkeley's genuine philosophical achievement (a relational, perceiver-dependent account of sensible qualities) while rejecting Berkeley's stronger metaphysical idealism (that reality is exhaustively mental).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell's own critical analysis of the Dialogues, contained in this chapter.
examples: Russell's 'nephew/uncle' analogy: it is logically necessary that a nephew has an uncle given that he is a nephew, but this proves nothing about whether Mr. A (who happens to be a nephew) could have existed without being anyone's nephew -- analogously, that a perceived object requires a perceiver does not show an object could not have existed unperceived
Russell's physicalist redefinition: an event is 'perceived' if it has effects of certain kinds (e.g., can be remembered), a definition that does not require any 'mental substance' at all
objections: Berkeley's logical arguments (e.g., 'whatever is immediately perceived is an idea; can any idea exist out of the mind?') commit a fallacy of assuming what needs to be proved
Berkeley's empirical arguments (e.g., heat as a 'pain,' therefore mental) trade on an ambiguity between the painful quality of a sensation and the sensation that has that quality
competing_positions: Berkeley's own idealism, that all reality is ultimately mental
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell uses this critique to develop his own neutral, physicalist account of 'mind' and 'matter' as different groupings of events, connected respectively by memory-chains or by the equations of physics.

core_concepts.name: Four positions on inference from percepts to unperceived events
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Once we accept that all we directly know are our own perceptions ('percepts'), there is a further question: can we validly infer that anything exists beyond those percepts -- other people's experiences, or even events that no one perceives at all (like furniture in a dark, empty room)? Russell lays out four increasingly generous answers to this question.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's four positions: (1) total denial of any inference beyond my own present percepts and memories (strict deductive scepticism); (2) solipsism, allowing inference only to other events in my own biography (e.g., unnoticed sense-data); (3) the view (attributed to Eddington) allowing inference, by analogy, to events in other minds, but not to events experienced by no one; (4) common sense and traditional physics, which infers to events that no one experiences at all (e.g., unobserved furniture), typically via causal laws.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell uses this taxonomy to reframe the Berkeley/idealism debate as fundamentally a question about the scope and validity of non-demonstrative (inductive/analogical) inference, rather than a question that can be settled by logic alone -- deferring final judgment to a later, fuller treatment of probability and induction.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell's own systematic analysis, developed in response to and building on Berkeley's arguments.
examples: G. E. Moore's jab at idealists supposedly believing 'trains only have wheels while they are in stations'
The dark bedroom example: does the furniture exist, unperceived, while I sleep?

arguments.title: The lukewarm water argument against the objectivity of heat and cold
premises: If one hand is hot and the other cold, and both are placed in the same lukewarm water, the water will feel cold to the hot hand and hot to the cold hand.
The water itself cannot be both hot and cold at once, if hot and cold are objective properties of the water.
Therefore what we call 'hot' and 'cold' must be sensations in the perceiver, not properties in the water itself.
arguments.conclusion: Heat and cold 'are only sensations existing in our minds,' not qualities inherent in objects.
arguments.explanation: This is Berkeley's most famous empirical argument (voiced by Philonous against Hylas), reinforcing an earlier argument that intense heat is itself a kind of pain, and pain must be mental.
objections: Russell notes this strictly proves only that what we perceive is 'hotter' or 'colder,' a comparative/relational fact, not that heat and cold as such are wholly subjective.
implications: Sets the pattern Berkeley repeats for taste, smell, and sound before extending the argument to primary qualities like extension and motion

arguments.title: Extension of the relativity argument from secondary to primary qualities
premises: Things look larger when we are near them and smaller when we are far away, yet a thing cannot have two different sizes at once if size is truly 'in' the object.
A given motion may appear fast to one observer and slow to another.
The same style of argument that showed secondary qualities (colour, taste, sound) are perceiver-relative applies equally to primary qualities like extension and motion.
arguments.conclusion: Primary qualities, no less than secondary ones, are mind-dependent, undermining Locke's distinction between qualities 'actually in bodies' and qualities 'only in the percipient.'
arguments.explanation: Russell judges these particular empirical arguments valid as proving the subjectivity of perceived space (size and speed genuinely do vary with the observer's position and frame of reference), but denies they prove primary qualities are 'mental,' since 'this subjectivity is physical: it is equally true of a camera.'
objections: Russell: a camera also registers different apparent sizes at different distances without being 'mental' in any interesting sense, so perspective-relativity alone does not establish mentality.
implications: Completes Berkeley's demolition of Locke's primary/secondary quality distinction, a key link to the previous chapter on Locke

arguments.title: The logical argument: 'whatever is immediately perceived is an idea'
premises: Whatever is immediately perceived by the senses is, by definition, an 'idea.'
An idea, Berkeley holds, cannot exist outside some mind.
Therefore any immediate object of the senses cannot exist outside a mind, exterior to all minds -- this would be 'in itself an evident contradiction.'
arguments.conclusion: Sensible objects necessarily exist only in minds; unperceived, mind-independent sensible objects are logically impossible.
arguments.explanation: Russell judges this the weakest of Berkeley's arguments, diagnosing a fallacy analogous to arguing that, because Mr. A happens to be a nephew, and nephews logically require uncles, it is therefore logically necessary that Mr. A have an uncle -- when in fact nothing about Mr. A himself requires this, only the concept 'nephew' as applied to him.
objections: Russell's nephew/uncle fallacy analogy: being a perceived object requires a perceiver by definition, but this says nothing about whether the same entity could have existed without being perceived

Russell's 'unperceived pebble' example: ordinary empirical concepts like 'pebble' do not build in the fact of being perceived, so 'unperceived pebble' is a logically coherent notion even if no instance of it could itself ever be perceived (by definition)
implications: If this argument fails, as Russell contends, Berkeley's idealism loses its strongest claim to logical necessity and is left resting only on the weaker empirical arguments

key_distinctions: Perceiving a 'thing' vs. perceiving bundles of sensible qualities
Primary qualities vs. secondary qualities (inherited from Locke, but collapsed by Berkeley)
Logical/a priori arguments vs. empirical arguments within Berkeley's case against matter
The act of perceiving vs. the object perceived
Four grades of inference from percepts: no inference; solipsistic inference; analogical inference to other minds; full inference to unperceived events
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Berkeley directly extends and radicalizes Locke's primary/secondary quality distinction (Chapter XIII), turning Locke's own style of argument against secondary qualities into a weapon against primary qualities as well, and adopts Locke's nominalism about general ideas as a starting premise in the Dialogues.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell notes Hegel later held, on different grounds, the same view that only minds and mental events can exist logically -- a view Russell calls 'a complete mistake' in both cases; Russell's own physicalist redefinitions of 'mind' and 'matter' (as groupings of events connected by memory or by the equations of physics) anticipate and set up the discussion of Hume's even more radical empiricism in the following chapter.
religion_science_culture_context: Berkeley's argument is explicitly bound up with natural theology: God's constant perception secures the continuous existence of the physical world, which Berkeley treats as itself evidence for God's existence; Russell also situates Berkeley's later turn to promoting tar-water as symptomatic of his move away from serious philosophy after the age of twenty-eight.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Berkeley as a brilliant, charming stylist whose central and most famous argument -- that material objects exist only through being perceived, with God's constant perception securing their continuity -- rests on a mixture of genuinely valid and seriously flawed reasoning. Working closely through the first Dialogue and the opening of the second, Russell credits Berkeley with a real philosophical advance: showing that we perceive only sensible qualities, relative to the perceiver, not some further 'thing' or 'substance' behind them. But Russell sharply distinguishes this valid conclusion from Berkeley's stronger, and in Russell's view unjustified, further claim that these relative qualities are therefore 'mental' -- a claim Russell traces to an unexamined assumption that everything must be either wholly material or wholly mental, and to a specific logical fallacy (illustrated by the nephew/uncle analogy) in Berkeley's core argument that 'whatever is immediately perceived is an idea.' Russell separately assesses Berkeley's empirical arguments (the pain-argument for heat/cold, the lukewarm-water argument, the near/far argument for size) as mostly valid for proving perceptual relativity, but not for proving mentality, since 'this subjectivity is physical: it is equally true of a camera.' The chapter closes with Russell's own constructive proposal: define 'mind' and 'matter' not as competing metaphysical substances but as different kinds of groupings of events -- mind via memory-chains, matter via satisfaction of physical equations -- a redefinition meant to dissolve rather than answer Berkeley's dichotomy.
critical_context: Common scholarly criticism, which Russell himself develops at length: Berkeley's central logical argument for idealism commits a fallacy of illicitly inferring that perceived objects could not exist unperceived merely from the fact that, as perceived, they require a perceiver -- a criticism widely echoed in the subsequent history of philosophy of perception. Later development: Russell's own proposal to define perception in terms of causal 'effects of certain kinds' (so that even a river valley might loosely be said to 'perceive' or 'remember' past rainfall) anticipates functionalist and physicalist approaches to mind that became influential well after Russell's own time.
key_takeaways: Berkeley denied the existence of matter, holding that material objects exist only through being perceived, with God's constant perception securing their continuous existence.
Berkeley's Dialogues of Hylas and Philonous dramatize his argument as a debate between common-sense realism (Hylas) and Berkeley's own idealism (Philonous).
Berkeley extended Locke's argument against the objectivity of secondary qualities (colour, sound, taste) to primary qualities (extension, motion) as well, collapsing Locke's distinction.
Russell accepts that we perceive only relative, perceiver-dependent qualities, not 'things' behind them, but rejects Berkeley's further claim that this makes those qualities inherently 'mental.'

Russell diagnoses a key logical fallacy in Berkeley's core argument ('whatever is immediately perceived is an idea'), analogous to wrongly inferring that a nephew's existence logically requires an uncle to exist in every possible respect.

Russell distinguishes four progressively more generous positions on what we may validly infer beyond our own immediate perceptions, from strict solipsism to full common-sense realism about unperceived events.
Russell proposes redefining 'mind' and 'matter' as different kinds of event-groupings (connected by memory, or by physical law) rather than as rival metaphysical substances.
study_notes:
The most important interpretive move in this chapter is Russell's separation of Berkeley's argument into two distinct claims with very different degrees of support. Claim one -- we perceive only sensible qualities, not some further 'substance' underlying them, and these qualities are relative to the perceiver's situation -- Russell regards as basically sound and important. Claim two -- that these qualities are therefore 'mental,' and hence that all reality is mental -- Russell regards as unsupported, resting on an undefined term ('mental') and a specific logical fallacy. Keep this two-part structure in mind throughout: almost every specific argument in the chapter (heat/cold, taste, sound, colour, extension, motion) is really an argument for claim one that Berkeley then over-interprets as an argument for claim two.

The nephew/uncle analogy is the single most useful tool for understanding Russell's core objection: from 'all perceived things require a perceiver' it does not follow that 'this particular thing could not have existed without being perceived' -- just as from 'all nephews have uncles' it does not follow that any particular man's existence logically requires an uncle to exist, only that if he is classified as a nephew, an uncle is implied by that classification, not built into his own nature.

Finally, track how this chapter sets up the following one on Hume. Russell's four-position taxonomy of inference from percepts (solipsism, analogical inference to other minds, and so on) is explicitly left unresolved here, pending 'an elaborate investigation of non-demonstrative inference and the theory of probability' -- exactly the territory Hume enters, more radically and more consistently than either Locke or Berkeley, in Chapter XVII.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Latin for 'to be is to be perceived' -- Berkeley's slogan for the idea that things only exist while some mind is perceiving them.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Berkeley's core idealist principle that the being (esse) of sensible objects consists entirely in their being perceived (percipi).

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The two characters in Berkeley's dialogue: Hylas defends ordinary belief in matter, Philonous (Berkeley's own view) argues him out of it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The two interlocutors of Berkeley's Dialogues Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, representing respectively scientifically educated common sense (Hylas) and Berkeley's immaterialist idealism (Philonous).

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The properties we actually perceive through our senses -- colours, sounds, tastes, textures -- as opposed to some hidden 'thing' supposedly behind them.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The immediate objects of sense perception (colour, sound, taste, etc.), which Berkeley and Russell agree are what we actually perceive, rather than any underlying material substance.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Reasoning that gives you a probable, but not logically certain, conclusion -- like inferring that other people have feelings, or that the sun will rise tomorrow.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Inference that is not strictly deductive (i.e., not logically guaranteed by its premises), including inductive and analogical inference, central to the question of what we can validly infer beyond our own immediate percepts.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The view that we can only really be sure of our own mind and experiences, not of other people's minds or an outside world.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Russell's taxonomy, the position allowing inference from present percepts only to other events within one's own biography, denying justified inference to other minds or to events no one perceives.

questions.prompt: What does Berkeley mean by claiming that material objects 'only exist through being perceived'?
questions.answer: That sensible things (trees, tables, rocks) have no existence independent of some mind perceiving them; their reality consists entirely in being perceived.
questions.explanation: This is Berkeley's central idealist doctrine, examined throughout the chapter via the Dialogues.

questions.prompt: How does Berkeley answer the objection that unperceived objects (like a tree in an empty quad) would seem to blink in and out of existence?
questions.answer: By arguing that God perceives everything at all times, so objects retain continuous existence via God's perpetual perception, even when no finite mind is observing them.
questions.explanation: Berkeley treats this need for a perpetual perceiver as itself an argument for God's existence.

questions.prompt: Which earlier philosopher's primary/secondary quality distinction does Berkeley's argument extend and ultimately collapse?
questions.explanation: Berkeley (via Philonous) shows that Locke's arguments against the objectivity of secondary qualities apply equally to Locke's supposedly objective primary qualities.

questions.prompt: Contrast what Russell thinks Berkeley actually proved with what Berkeley thought he had proved.
questions.answer: Russell thinks Berkeley proved that we perceive only sensible qualities (not 'things' or substances), and that these qualities are relative to the perceiver. Berkeley thought he had proved that all reality is mental -- a stronger claim Russell rejects as resting on an undefined notion of 'mental' and on a specific logical fallacy.
questions.explanation: This distinction is the chapter's central interpretive thesis.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's 'nephew and uncle' objection to Berkeley's claim that 'whatever is immediately perceived is an idea, and can any idea exist out of the mind?'
questions.answer: Berkeley argues that since perceived objects are, by definition, objects of perception, they cannot exist unperceived -- just as, Russell notes, it is logically necessary for a nephew to have an uncle, given that he is classified as a nephew. But this necessity comes only from the definition/classification itself, not from anything intrinsic to the entity in question; so it does not follow that the same object could not have existed without ever being perceived, just as Mr. A's own nature does not require that he have an uncle.
questions.explanation: Russell regards this as exposing the central fallacy in Berkeley's strongest logical argument for idealism.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, why doesn't the fact that perceived size varies with distance (or perceived speed with the observer) prove that extension and motion are 'mental'?
questions.answer: Because this kind of relativity is purely physical and applies equally to non-mental instruments, like a camera, which also registers different apparent sizes at different distances without thereby being 'mental.'
questions.explanation: This shows Russell accepting the relativity of primary qualities to perspective while rejecting the further inference to mentality.

questions.prompt: Compare the four positions Russell distinguishes for inferring from our own percepts to other events, from most restrictive to most permissive.
questions.answer: (1) No inference at all beyond present percepts and memories; (2) solipsism, allowing inference only to other events in one's own biography; (3) analogical inference to events in other minds (e.g., other people's sensations), but not to wholly unperceived events; (4) common sense and physics, which infer to events no one perceives at all, typically via causal laws.
questions.explanation: Russell lays these out systematically before declining, in this chapter, to decide definitively among them.

flashcards.front: What is Berkeley's central doctrine about material objects?
flashcards.back: That material objects only exist through being perceived (esse est percipi); apart from perception, there is no matter.

flashcards.front: How does Berkeley explain the continuous existence of unperceived objects?
flashcards.back: God perceives everything at all times, so objects continue to exist via God's constant perception even when no finite mind observes them.

flashcards.front: Who are the two characters in Berkeley's Dialogues, and what do they represent?
flashcards.back: Hylas represents scientifically educated common sense (belief in matter); Philonous is Berkeley's own mouthpiece, arguing against matter.

flashcards.front: What is the lukewarm water argument meant to show?
flashcards.back: That heat and cold cannot be objective properties of water, since the same water feels hot to one hand and cold to the other simultaneously.

flashcards.front: How does Berkeley extend his argument from secondary to primary qualities?
flashcards.back: By showing that primary qualities like extension and motion also vary with the observer (near/far, fast/slow to different observers), just as secondary qualities do.

flashcards.front: What does Russell say Berkeley actually proved, as opposed to what he thought he proved?
flashcards.back: Berkeley proved we perceive qualities (not things), relative to the perceiver -- not, as he believed, that all reality is mental.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's 'nephew and uncle' analogy meant to refute?
flashcards.back: Berkeley's claim that because perceived objects are, by definition, objects of perception, they cannot logically exist unperceived.

flashcards.front: Why does Russell say the relativity of perceived size (near/far) does not prove extension is 'mental'?
flashcards.back: Because this relativity is purely physical and applies equally to non-mental devices like a camera.

flashcards.front: What later philosopher does Russell say also held that only minds can exist, on different grounds?
What is G. E. Moore's jab at idealists that Russell cites?
flashcards.back: That idealists seem to believe 'trains only have wheels while they are in stations,' since passengers cannot see the wheels while riding.

flashcards.front: List Russell's four positions on inference from percepts to unperceived events, from most to least restrictive.
flashcards.back: (1) No inference at all; (2) solipsism (inference only within one's own biography); (3) analogical inference to other minds; (4) common-sense/physics inference to wholly unperceived events.

flashcards.front: How does Russell propose to redefine 'matter' once substance is rejected?
flashcards.back: As what satisfies the equations of physics -- a logical construction out of events, not a metaphysical substance.

flashcards.front: How does Russell propose to redefine 'mind' once substance is rejected?
flashcards.back: As a group or structure of events connected by memory-chains, forwards or backwards.

flashcards.front: What did Berkeley turn to promoting in his later life, after abandoning serious philosophy?
flashcards.back: Tar-water, which he believed had marvellous medicinal properties.

quiz.prompt: Berkeley's famous doctrine holds that material objects:
options: Are made of atoms in a void
quiz.explanation: Berkeley's esse est percipi doctrine holds that to be, for a sensible thing, is to be perceived.
quiz.related_concept: The denial of the existence of matter

quiz.prompt: In Berkeley's Dialogues, which character represents Berkeley's own view?
quiz.explanation: Philonous is Berkeley's mouthpiece; Hylas represents common-sense belief in matter.
quiz.related_concept: The Dialogues' method: Hylas and Philonous

quiz.prompt: True or False: Berkeley uses God's constant perception to explain why objects continue to exist when no human is observing them.
quiz.explanation: Berkeley holds that God always perceives everything, securing the continuity of unperceived objects.
quiz.related_concept: God as guarantor of the continuity of unperceived objects

quiz.prompt: What does the lukewarm water argument attempt to show?
options: That heat and cold are not objective properties of objects
That primary qualities are always accurate
That the senses never deceive us
quiz.explanation: The same water feeling hot to one hand and cold to another is used to argue heat/cold are sensations, not objective properties.
quiz.related_concept: The Dialogues' method: Hylas and Philonous

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, what is the key flaw in Berkeley's claim that 'whatever is immediately perceived is an idea, and can any idea exist out of the mind'?
options: It commits a fallacy analogous to assuming a nephew's own nature requires an uncle to exist
It was never actually argued by Berkeley
quiz.explanation: Russell's nephew/uncle analogy shows the argument mistakes a definitional/relational necessity for a necessity intrinsic to the object itself.
quiz.related_concept: Russell's critique: qualities are relative, not necessarily 'mental'

quiz.prompt: Russell argues the perspectival relativity of size and motion is merely ____, not proof that these qualities are mental, since it applies equally to a camera.
quiz.explanation: Russell distinguishes physical relativity (true of cameras too) from genuine mentality.
quiz.related_concept: Russell's critique: qualities are relative, not necessarily 'mental'

quiz.prompt: Which of Russell's four positions on inference from percepts corresponds to solipsism as ordinarily understood?
options: Denying all inference beyond present percepts
Allowing inference only to other events in one's own biography
Allowing inference to events in other minds by analogy
Allowing inference to wholly unperceived events
quiz.explanation: Russell's second position, solipsism, permits inference to unnoticed events within one's own experience but not beyond it.
quiz.related_concept: Four positions on inference from percepts to unperceived events

quiz.prompt: True or False: Russell agrees with Berkeley and Hegel that there are logical reasons proving only minds and mental events can exist.
